1366.title: Choirs
1366.howItsDone: Church choirs come in different forms: robed cathedral and parish choirs, gospel choirs, Orthodox choirs that sing the whole liturgy, and small groups of volunteers who rehearse during the week and lead the congregation's singing on Sunday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, organs, guitars and drums, and a psalm that ends on breath. Your line was every instrument praise.

Four people stand in a row, each singing a different note. Alone, the low note sounds gloomy. The high one sounds thin. The two in the middle sound like they've lost the tune. Then they sing at the same moment, and the four odd notes become one chord, full and warm, that none of them could make alone. That's the whole secret of a choir: a cathedral choir in white robes, a gospel choir swaying on the beat, an Orthodox choir singing a service from start to finish, six faithful people in a village church.

Start at the temple. When Solomon's temple is dedicated, Chronicles says: "It came even to pass, as the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the LORD." Then, the story says, the house was filled with a cloud. The singing comes first; the glory follows. Next, one mouth, many voices. Paul writes to the Christians in Rome: "That ye may with one mind and one mouth glorify God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." One mouth sounds like everyone saying the same thing. But in a choir, sopranos, altos, tenors and basses each sing a different line, and the unity is in the harmony, not in sameness. If everyone sang the melody, you'd lose the chord. Then, a choir on a wall. In Nehemiah, Jerusalem's broken walls have been rebuilt, and Nehemiah sets two great companies of singers giving thanks on top of the wall. They go opposite ways and meet at the house of God: two choirs, singing a city back to life. Last, near the Bible's end, John hears heaven in Revelation: "And I heard as it were the voice of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunderings, saying, Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth." Countless voices, each its own, poured into one sound. In this scene, heaven doesn't whisper. It sings.

If someone's with you, hum a tune you both know, a hymn or a lullaby, and listen for the moment your voices meet. If you're alone, hum one part along with a choir recording, the low line or the high one, and notice how it fits inside the whole. If you pray, you can let the song be your prayer alongside other voices; if you don't, listen for the place where many voices become one sound.
Choirs. Many voices, each holding its own part, making one sound to praise God.
Your line: many voices. Each one holds its own part, and the chord needs all of them. See you next time.

1367.title: Churches around the world
1367.hook: from Ethiopian round churches to Korean hilltop crosses
1367.howItsDone: Christians around the world worship in buildings of many shapes: round churches and rock-hewn churches in Ethiopia, domed churches in the Orthodox world, Gothic cathedrals, white wooden chapels, and churches above shops in Korean cities marked by lit crosses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, choirs: four odd notes that turn into one chord. Your line was many voices.

On a green Ethiopian hillside, a church stands in a ring of old trees. Its walls make a circle, its roof rises to a point, and people in white shawls stand outside the doors and pray toward the center. Now cross the world to a Korean city after dark. From a high window, red crosses glow on rooftops all over the hills, like a field of small lit signs. Same faith, two very different buildings. Neither looks like the white steeple some people picture when they hear the word church.
screen: `A ROUND CHURCH IN A RING OF TREES.`

segments.voice: Start with a promise in Acts. Before Jesus is taken up, he tells his friends: "ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth." A few chapters later, the story leaves the map. An official from Ethiopia, riding home in his chariot and reading the prophet Isaiah, meets Philip on a desert road. They pass water, and the man says: "See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?" Next, the round church. In the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, some churches are built in a circle, rings within rings, with the most holy place at the very center, where only priests go. The building is a map of drawing near to God: outer ring, inner ring, heart. In Lalibela, tradition says, churches were carved straight down into solid rock. Then the lit crosses. In Korea, crosses glowing red or white at night mark churches across the cities. A church there might be a single floor above a shop. The shape is new; the prayer inside is the same old prayer. Last, a conversation at a well. A Samaritan woman asks Jesus which mountain is the right place to worship. He answers: "the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father." No one mountain, no one shape. A church in the rock, in a ring of trees or above a shop can bear the same name.
screen: `TO THE UTTERMOST PART OF THE EARTH.`
`A ROUND CHURCH, THE HOLY PLACE AT ITS HEART.`

segments.voice: Find a photo of a church far from where you live, a round church in Ethiopia, a wooden church in the far north, a church in a Korean city, and look slowly: the doors, where the light comes in, what's at the center. Then imagine the people who'll walk in this week, and what they'll carry with them. If you pray, you can pray for that congregation; if you don't, simply hold them in mind for a moment.
Churches around the world. Round, carved, domed, lit up at night: the many shapes the same faith takes in different places.
Your line: many shapes. One faith, built in many places. See you tomorrow.

1368.title: Crosses of many lands
1368.howItsDone: Christians in different lands carry the cross in their own forms: Celtic high crosses with a ring, small crosses tattooed on the wrist by some Coptic Christians, Ethiopian hand crosses carried by priests to bless people, and three-barred crosses in Russian and other Orthodox churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, churches around the world: round, carved, lit up at night. Your line was many shapes.

On the inside of a wrist, just below the palm, a small blue cross, inked into the skin. It doesn't wash off. Some Coptic Christians in Egypt wear one for life. Lay other crosses beside it. A gray stone cross in an Irish field, taller than a man, with a ring around its center. A silver cross from Ethiopia, held in a priest's hand, its arms opening into patterns like lace. A cross from a Russian church with three bars, the lowest one slanting. Four lands, four shapes, all pointing to the same cross.
screen: `A RING, A LACE, A SLANTED BAR.`

segments.voice: Start in Ireland and Scotland, with the Celtic cross: a ring around the place where the arms meet. What did the ring first mean? Some see a halo, some the sun, some a circle with no end; others think it helped hold the stone arms up. The stone doesn't explain itself. Next, Egypt. Some Coptic Christians carry a small cross tattooed on the inner wrist, some from childhood: a way of belonging that can't be taken off. Paul wrote to the Galatians, "I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus." Many readers take him to mean his scars. A wrist cross is a gentler mark, worn in the same spirit. Then Ethiopia. Priests there may carry a hand cross of metal or wood, its arms opening into woven patterns, and people come up to kiss it and be blessed. Styles differ from place to place and maker to maker. Last, the Russian Orthodox cross. The top bar stands for Pilate's sign. John says: "And Pilate wrote a title, and put it on the cross. And the writing was, JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS." When the chief priests asked him to change it, Pilate said: "What I have written I have written." The slanted bottom bar is a footrest, and Orthodox tradition says it tilts up toward the thief who asked to be remembered. Under them all, one line from Luke: "If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me."

With pen and paper, draw one cross from another land, the Celtic ring, the Orthodox slanted foot, or an Ethiopian cross's patterned arms, and give its one special detail your care. As you draw, think of the people who carry that shape: in a field, on a wrist, in a priest's hand. If you pray, you can pray for them as you draw; if you don't, let the drawing be a way of paying attention to strangers.
Crosses of many lands. Ringed, inked, woven, three-barred: one cross, shaped by the places that carry it.
Your line: many crosses. Each land shaped the same sign its own way. Until tomorrow.

1369.title: Name days
1369.hook: many Orthodox and Catholic Christians celebrate their saint's day
1369.howItsDone: Some Orthodox and Catholic Christians celebrate the feast day of the saint they are named for, often with church in the morning, a family meal and visits from friends; in Orthodox tradition a child is often given a saint's name at baptism.

segments.voice: Yesterday, crosses of many lands: ringed, inked, woven, three-barred. Your line was many crosses.

A phone buzzes before breakfast. Then again, and again. By lunch, a man named Nikos has a stack of messages, a call from his aunt, and a tray of pastries waiting at work. It isn't his birthday. It's his name day: the feast of Saint Nicholas, the saint he's named for. Tonight, friends may drop by without being invited, because on a name day, in his family, the door is open. In some Orthodox and Catholic families, a name day is celebrated as warmly as a birthday.

In Catholic and Orthodox life, saints are remembered on particular days of the year. If you're named for a saint, that saint's day becomes your day too. Some go to church that morning; some families eat together. The saint is a companion, someone who walked the road before you. Hebrews pictures the faithful who came before as a crowd in the stands: "we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses." A name day picks one face out of that cloud and says: this one is yours. Next, a naming in Luke. Elizabeth has a son in her old age, and the neighbors want to call him Zacharias, after his father. Elizabeth says no, he'll be called John. Zacharias, who can't speak, asks for a writing tablet: "His name is John. And they marvelled all." In John's Gospel, Jesus gives Simon a new name: "thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone." A name, and a calling with it. Then Isaiah: "Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine." Isaiah speaks to Israel, a whole people, and still the phrase is personal. Last, Revelation, the Bible's last book: the one who overcomes is given "a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it." Not every church keeps name days; others honor the saints in other ways. But the thread holds: in this faith, a name has a story.
screen: `I HAVE CALLED THEE BY THY NAME.`

segments.voice: Think about your own name: who gave it to you, and why, and whether a saint shares it, or part of it. Some names have no saint, and they still have a story. If you pray, you can hear Isaiah's words, I have called thee by thy name, as spoken to you; if you don't, just sit with the name you've carried all your life.
screen: `I HAVE CALLED THEE BY THY NAME.`

Your line: your name has a story. Someone gave it to you on purpose. See you tomorrow.

1370.title: Grace at meals
1370.hook: bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts
1370.howItsDone: Christians of different churches say a short grace before meals, at home or in public; Catholics often use "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts," others use their own set words or pray in their own words, and some also give thanks after eating.

segments.voice: Yesterday, name days: a phone that buzzed all morning for Saint Nicholas. Your line was your name has a story.

"Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts." At one kitchen table, a family says it so fast it comes out as one long word, and the youngest is reaching for the potatoes before the amen. At another, an old couple hold hands across the plates and say it slowly, the way they've said it for years. In a school cafeteria, a girl bows her head for two seconds over a tray, and nobody notices but her. The words are short. The food is getting cold. And still, people stop, just before the first bite.

The old Catholic grace goes: "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen." It doesn't call the food dinner. It calls it gifts, named as given before anyone has tasted it. Other churches have their own graces, rhymed or spoken freely, but they tend to do the same thing. Next, Jesus at a meal. In Mark, a hungry crowd sits on the grass with almost nothing to eat. The disciples want to send everyone away to buy food. Instead, Jesus takes what there is: "he looked up to heaven, and blessed, and brake the loaves." Look up, bless, break: a pause, a word of thanks, and then the food is shared. Then, an older command. In Deuteronomy, Moses tells the people: "When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God for the good land which he hath given thee." After the meal, when you're full, exactly when it's easiest to forget. Jewish tradition keeps a blessing after eating from this verse; Christian graces come before the meal, after it, or both. Last, Paul to Timothy: "For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving." Grace doesn't change the food. It changes how the food is received.
screen: `BLESS US, O LORD, AND THESE THY GIFTS.`
`HE LOOKED UP, AND BLESSED, AND BRAKE.`
`WHEN THOU HAST EATEN AND ART FULL.`

segments.voice: Set food or a drink in front of you, or bring your next meal to mind, and trace it backward, one breath for each step: the hands that cooked it, the store, the truck, the field, the rain. If you pray, you can say the old grace slowly, one phrase at a time; if you don't, silently name a few of the people it took to bring this food to you.
screen: `BLESS US, O LORD, AND THESE THY GIFTS.`

Your line: these thy gifts. A meal, named as given. Same time tomorrow.

1371.title: Bedtime prayers
1371.hook: Now I lay me down to sleep: children's prayers carried for life
1371.howItsDone: Some Christian parents teach children a short prayer to say at bedtime, such as "Now I lay me down to sleep"; Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants also have longer evening and night prayers, said at home or in church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, grace at meals, said by one family so fast it came out as one long word. Your line was these thy gifts.

The bedroom light is off. Only the hallway lamp is on, and the door is open a crack. A small voice comes from under a blanket: "Now I lay me down to sleep, I pray the Lord my soul to keep." A parent sits on the edge of the bed and says it along. Years go by. The child grows up and stops saying it. Then one night, in a strange bed, a hospital, a hotel, the night before something hard, the words come back on their own.
screen: `NOW I LAY ME DOWN TO SLEEP.`

segments.voice: In its old form, the children's prayer goes: "Now I lay me down to sleep, I pray the Lord my soul to keep; If I should die before I wake, I pray the Lord my soul to take." It isn't a Bible verse, and its third line can startle a modern parent. Some families keep it; some swap in a gentler line. Before letting go of the day, a child hands themselves over to God's keeping. Next, the Psalms. One psalm's heading sets it when David fled from Absalom, his own son, and it says: "I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me." Enemies all around, and he sleeps. Another psalm ends: "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety." Lying down becomes an act of trust. Then, the one who doesn't sleep. Psalm one hundred twenty-one: "Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep." You can close your eyes because someone else is keeping watch. Last, the grown-up version. The old English prayer book gives the church an evening prayer: "Lighten our darkness, we beseech thee, O Lord; and by thy great mercy defend us from all perils and dangers of this night." The child's request, in longer words. Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants each have their own night prayers, alone or together. For some, the children's prayer is still the one that comes first in the dark.
screen: `NOW I LAY ME DOWN TO SLEEP.`
`I LAID ME DOWN AND SLEPT; I AWAKED.`

segments.voice: Lie down if it's night, or sit back and let your shoulders drop as if it were, and let the day go one piece at a time: the conversations, the tasks, the thing you didn't finish. If you pray, you can say the children's prayer or the psalm on the screen slowly, the way you'd hand something to someone you trust; if you don't, notice what it would feel like to set the whole day down and let someone else keep watch.
screen: `I WILL BOTH LAY ME DOWN IN PEACE, AND SLEEP.`

1372.title: The icon corner
1372.hook: Orthodox homes keep a beautiful corner for prayer
1372.howItsDone: Some Orthodox Christians keep an icon corner at home, with icons, a lamp and a prayer book, and pray there in the morning and evening; some Catholic families keep a home altar, and other Christians keep a quiet chair or shelf for prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bedtime prayers, handing over the night. Your line was keep me through the night.

Up near the ceiling, in a living-room corner, a small shelf. On it, a few painted faces on wood: Christ, his mother, a saint or two. A little oil lamp flickers in red glass. A dried palm branch is tucked behind one frame. On the other wall, the television; on the table, homework and keys. Nobody here built a chapel. They gave one corner of an ordinary room a different job. Some Orthodox families pray before a shelf like this, morning and night.
screen: `FACES ON WOOD, A LAMP IN RED GLASS.`

segments.voice: In Russian homes it has been called the beautiful corner, and other Orthodox families keep their own versions. Tradition puts it on the east wall where the room allows, toward the sunrise. Icons of Christ and Mary sit there, often with the saints the family are named for. It's small on purpose: a shelf, not a shrine room. Jesus, in the Sermon on the Mount: "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret." A closet there means an inner room; Jesus is warning against prayer put on for an audience. In a corner at home, nobody is watching but the faces on the shelf. Then, the habit. In Daniel, a new law forbids prayer to anyone but the king, and Daniel goes home anyway: "his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime." A room, a direction, a time, and a habit there before the trouble came. Last, Jacob, running from his brother, dreams of a ladder reaching to heaven. He wakes and says, "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not," and, "this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." The icon corner says the same about a living room. Other Christians keep their own versions: a Catholic home altar with a crucifix and a statue of Mary, or a chair by the window with a worn Bible on the arm. The shape changes; the idea holds.

Look around and choose one spot, a shelf, a windowsill, and in your mind clear it and set one thing there: a cross, an icon, a candle, a Bible, or a photo of someone you want to remember. If you pray, you can pray there in your own words or your church's, the way Daniel kept his window; if you don't, let it be a corner kept for quiet.
The icon corner. A small place at home set apart for prayer, with icons, a lamp, and the things a family holds holy.
Your line: a corner of heaven. One small spot, kept for prayer. Until morning.
